title: China's churches
hook: registered and house churches, growing through persecution

segments.voice: Yesterday, saebyeok gido, a room praying aloud before sunrise, and your line was dawn prayer.

Two Sunday mornings in the same Chinese city. In the first, a church with its name on the gate: doors open, choir robed, hymn numbers on a board at the front, registered with the state. In the second, an apartment a few streets away. Curtains drawn. Folding chairs borrowed from neighbors who don't ask questions. Someone keeps the singing soft. Both rooms are reading the same Gospel. Both are being watched, in different ways.
screen: `A CHURCH WITH ITS NAME ON THE GATE.`

segments.voice: Christians in China gather in roughly two ways. Registered churches belong to bodies the government recognizes, and meet openly under state rules about what can be taught and who can attend. House churches meet outside that system, in homes, offices, rented rooms. The line between them isn't always neat, and Christians in China disagree about it honestly. Some register so they can worship in the open and serve within the law. Others refuse, because they won't let the state decide what happens in worship. Reports from China describe hard seasons for both: crosses taken down from church roofs, gatherings closed, pastors detained. And still the people keep meeting. Nobody can count them exactly; a church in a living room keeps no public list. Jesus talked about growth you can't watch. In John's Gospel, in the King James Bible: "Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." A corn of wheat is just a grain. It goes under before anything comes up. And in Mark, a man scatters seed and goes to bed, and it grows while he sleeps and wakes: "the seed should spring and grow up, he knoweth not how." The farmer isn't in charge of it. An old saying, traced to an early Christian writer named Tertullian, says the blood of Christians is seed. Christians in China wouldn't all put it that way, and the old line is no reason to romanticize suffering. Some readers hear the same picture in what Jesus said: under the ground is not the same as gone.
screen: `A CORN OF WHEAT FALLS INTO THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Picture the two rooms from the start, and someone in each: an older woman with a worn Bible, a young man keeping one eye on the door. You don't know their names; hold them anyway. If you pray, pray for Christians in China in both kinds of room, in whatever words you have; if not, simply wish them safety and courage.
China's churches. Registered churches meeting in the open, and house churches meeting outside registration: two ways of gathering, under pressure, around the same Gospel.
Your line: the seed underground. Some growing happens where no one can watch it. Day nine hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Some Christians elsewhere pray for the church in China in their own prayers and in services; in China, registered congregations meet in church buildings, while house churches gather in homes and other private spaces.

chat.says: Do Christians in China all belong to one government church, or are they hidden?
options: Both ways: some meet in registered churches, others in house churches outside it.
All of them meet in secret, since every church in China is banned.
All of them belong to one church run openly by the government.
chat.meaning: Registered churches meet openly under state rules; house churches meet outside that system. Christians in China honestly disagree about which way is right.

notes: Claims rule: no numbers, growth figures or dates given; the index hook's 'growing' is rendered as 'still the people keep meeting' and 'nobody can count them exactly'. Confirm this is fair to the outline.

Registered churches are not named (Three-Self Patriotic Movement / China Christian Council for Protestants; the Catholic Patriotic Association and the unregistered Catholic communities are not discussed). A Keeper may want a sentence on Catholics in China.

'Reports from China describe ... crosses taken down from church roofs, gatherings closed, pastors detained': widely reported (e.g. Zhejiang cross removals, Early Rain Covenant Church), but no specifics or dates given; confirm wording is fair and not inflammatory.
The two stances on registration are described without ranking; confirm fairness to both.

Tertullian, Apology 50: the Latin is usually rendered 'the blood of Christians is seed'; the popular 'blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church' is a later paraphrase. Paraphrased with quoted: null; confirm.
The hook scene (a registered church and an apartment house church in one city) is illustrative, not a specific report.
